paper_metadata.title: Call Option Pricing Using Quantum Amplitude Estimation: A Comparative Study with Monte Carlo Simulation

summary: The paper studies Iterative Amplitude Estimation (IAE) for European call option pricing on Qiskit simulators and IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_brisbane), comparing against Monte Carlo with 100,000 trials and the Black–Scholes analytical benchmark. Reported errors are small: Monte Carlo absolute error is about 0.0077, QAE simulator error about 0.0080, and quantum results remain within 0.02 of the analytical price, but the hardware runs show wider confidence intervals (~0.029) and no demonstrated practical advantage.

experiments.description: Iterative Amplitude Estimation (IAE) for European call option pricing, evaluated on Qiskit simulator and IBM Quantum hardware, compared against Monte Carlo and Black–Scholes baselines.

algorithm.variant: Iterative Amplitude Estimation (IAE) for option pricing

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Log-normal distribution of terminal asset price S_T discretized over [L,H] covering three standard deviations of the log-normal mean; encoded into an n-qubit register. Payoff encoded with an ancilla qubit via controlled rotations.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate C = e^{-rT} E[(S_T-K)+] via amplitude estimation, then recover option price as C = e^{-rT} · a · B, where a is the estimated amplitude and B is the payoff scaling factor.

problem_instance.description: European call option pricing under risk-neutral GBM dynamics.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: GBM log-normal terminal price distribution discretized over a bounded interval; Monte Carlo uses 100,000 trials with fixed seed 42

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Sample Z ~ N(0,1); generate S_T = S0 exp((r - 1/2 sigma^2)T + sigma sqrt(T) Z); discretize terminal distribution for quantum state preparation; normalize payoff for ancilla encoding.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Simulator and hardware runs compared to Monte Carlo and Black–Scholes; absolute error, relative error, confidence intervals, runtime/resources reported.

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise / gate errors / qubit noise

implementation_details.classical_solver: Monte Carlo simulation and Black–Scholes analytical formula as baselines
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Monte Carlo implemented with NumPy and SciPy; Qiskit Finance, Qiskit Algorithms, and Qiskit Aer used for quantum implementation
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Clopper–Pearson intervals used in IAE; option price recovered from estimated amplitude and scaling factor B

speedup_claims.conditions: Iterative Amplitude Estimation (IAE) for expectation estimation / option pricing
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the asymptotic advantage O(1/ε) vs O(1/ε^2), but hardware results are affected by noise, discretization, and limited qubit depth.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; paper reports only a small-scale 1-underlying-asset option-pricing instance with 3-4 state qubits plus 1 ancilla
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: More qubits for richer state preparation, lower noise, deeper circuits, and efficient data loading for larger asset/state discretizations
limiting_factors: Noise and gate errors on IBM Brisbane hardware
Limited qubit depth and discretization error
No demonstrated runtime or cost advantage over Monte Carlo

notes: num_qubits inferred as 4 from the paper's stated hardware-friendly setup of 3-4 qubits for state encoding plus 1 ancilla qubit for payoff encoding; exact total register size is not explicitly stated.
circuit_depth not explicitly quantified; only reduced circuit depth / limited qubit depth is discussed.
The paper reports QAE estimates close to Monte Carlo and Black-Scholes, with absolute errors around 0.0077 (Monte Carlo) and 0.0080 (QAE simulator), but does not show a practical quantum advantage.
Hardware results are noisier and wider in confidence interval (~0.029), so the evidence supports parity/feasibility rather than advantage.
